images.notes: Left-hand of the two vertical strip drawings on printed page 233 (IA leaf n244; IIIF image _0245; crop x0–905 of the page). Block-by-block perspective line drawing with printed house numbers on the curb line: 1702, 1712, 1720, 1726, 1730, 1736, '18th St.', 1800 (Glessner, with its arched entry and 18th-Street wall), 1808, 1812. Shows uniform setbacks, front lawns, a continuous line of curbside posts/lamp-or-hitching posts and street trees, a carriage in the roadway. Drawn c.1892–93: 1702 here is the pre-Glessner-Lee-townhouse house (pa-1702-43, demolished before 1904) and 1726 is the early house later replaced, so for 1904 this is evidence of the earlier generation at those two lots; 1720, 1736, 1800–1812 are the buildings standing in 1904. Diagrammatic — façades are simplified and proportions not reliable for measurement; treat as a numbered sequence/massing guide.

images.camera_position: from the west side of Prairie Avenue opposite 1721, in winter
images.creator: George Glessner
images.repository: Glessner House Museum (George Glessner photographs; per blog caption)

images.rights_basis: Museum photograph reproduced on blog; no rights statement
images.notes: Winter view by George Glessner (the Glessners' son, an amateur photographer) of the 1863 frame Dexter house BEFORE Arthur Little's 1889 brick front addition: two-storey clapboard house with central front gable (round attic window), shuttered windows, bracketed eaves, a square cupola/belvedere and several tall chimneys, ground-floor bays, a low stone wall along the sidewalk with gate piers, a gas street lamp in the foreground; the neighbouring house at right (south, toward Pullman) shows brick bays. Because the 1889 addition was built nearly to the lot line, the 1904 frontage looked very different; this documents the original block that stood behind the addition until a later owner demolished it.

images.title: The Pullman residence, Chicago
images.camera_position: from the southwest corner of Prairie Avenue and 18th Street, looking across the intersection; 18th Street recedes to the right toward the Fort Dearborn Massacre monument
images.creator: Detroit Publishing Co.
images.repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division
images.rights_basis: LoC: No known restrictions on publication
images.notes: Glass negative ('286' on negative; holder note 'Prarie Avenue'). Date bracket from Detroit Catalogue J (1901); the Fort Dearborn Massacre monument (erected 1893) is visible at the far right end of 18th Street, so the view is 1893 or later. The best in-period full view of the Pullman house's west (Prairie) and south (18th St) fronts: three-storey ashlar Second Empire block with mansard, iron roof cresting, pedimented dormers, ivy-covered walls, columned entrance porch on Prairie, corner/side porch on 18th, low stone-capped wall with piers along both sidewalks, lamp posts, young elms on parkway, unpaved/macadam roadway with stone crosswalk slabs and a carriage at the 18th St kerb. At the left edge, the neighbouring house to the north (1721 Prairie, Wirt Dexter house, identification by position) shows a broad columned front porch, gabled dormers and tall chimneys — useful for the Dexter house's 1889 Arthur Little front. Leafless trees: autumn/spring.

images.notes: Engraving of the Fort Dearborn 'massacre tree' (cottonwood on the north side of 18th St east of Prairie, felled May 1894) with, at left, the Pullman coach house/stable: brick building with arched openings, patterned slate mansard with round-headed dormers, iron roof cresting and a small cupola, enclosed by a fence; open lakeshore with sailboats and a lamp post beyond. Probably a plate from a published history (Andreas, History of Chicago vol. 1, 1884, carries a massacre-tree illustration — not yet matched). Documents the Pullman stable on 18th Street; the tree was gone by 1904 and the monument (1893) stood nearby.

images.notes: Hunt office drawing ('No. 2, office copy'; inscribed 'M. Field' and 'Plan of Principal Floor'; 'This drawing to be returned to R. M. Hunt Archt.'), ink and wash with red-tinted masonry walls and a scale bar. Shows the principal-floor plan of the Field house: canted/octagonal-cornered rooms, a large circular stair hall projecting at the top of the sheet, a curved bay (hatched) on one side, and the entrance steps at the bottom of the sheet (the street front; the house stood on the east side of Prairie, facing west). The only Hunt drawing for the Field house LoC has digitized (searches 'Marshall and Nannie S. Field', 'Hunt Field residence Chicago', 'Richard Morris Hunt Chicago' all return only this plan). A design-stage drawing: as-built and any 1873–1904 changes need confirming against the 1886/1911 Sanborn footprints. Published as fig. 3.16b in Sam Watters, The Gilded Life of Richard Morris Hunt (2024). Scale bar on sheet — footprint dimensions could be measured from the TIFF (master: tile.loc.gov/storage-services/master/pnp/ppmsca/58300/58353u.tif).

FIELD', 'House for Marshall Field — Chicago Ill.', 'Plan of Principal Floor', 'Scale 1/4" = 1 ft', stamped 'This Drawing to be returned to R.M. Hunt Archt.' Rooms named: Drawing Room, Parlor(?), Library, Hall, Dining Room (octagonal), Conservatory (segmental bay), Main Stairs (circular, ~30 risers numbered), Service Stairs, Butler's Pantry, Closet; front entrance stoop and side steps drawn. images.title: Second Presbyterian Church, HABS No. IL-328: written historical and descriptive data
images.creator: Stephanie Gawur and Emily Wallrath, SAIC Historic Preservation Program, for HABS
images.repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division
images.rights_basis: No known restrictions on images made by the U.S. Government; images copied from other sources may be restricted (LoC HABS rights statement)
images.notes: 3-page HABS report (read in full). Exterior: Gothic Revival, cream-coloured, tar-stained rusticated Joliet limestone on south and east facades, common brick on north and west; prominent bell tower at SE corner; pointed-arch windows N and S; non-traditional two-aisle plan. History: Renwick building completed 1874; 1900 fire completely destroyed the sanctuary roof and smoke/water-damaged the nave; Howard Van Doren Shaw (a member) redesigned the interior in Arts and Crafts style (altered arches, supports and ceilings; art glass; murals; 175 angels; electrified fixtures); Frederic Clay Bartlett tree-of-life mural behind the choir loft. Coordinates 41.855696 N, -87.624367 W. NRHP 74000754. No numeric dimensions in the text (the 22 sheets carry them).

images.notes: Coarse-screen halftone captioned 'Shirley T. High Residence'. Shows a three-storey dark brick house with a steep front gable, a round corner tower with conical roof at left, arched entrance up a stone stoop, tall chimney, and a broad north side wing with a second gable; picket fence at right. This form is Queen Anne/Richardsonian of the 1880s — consistent with J. L. images.notes: Companion text to the four strip drawings. p. 232: drive turns off Michigan Boulevard 'and reach by Sixteenth Street — Prairie Avenue, a neighborhood of millionaires'; names Pullman 1729, Field 1905, Pike 2101. p. 234: Pullman residence description (remodelled 1892 with picture gallery and palm-house; conservatory and lawn on the south side of 18th St. toward Calumet; the Fort Dearborn massacre cottonwood and the Massacre Monument at the foot of 18th St.); 'From Eighteenth to Twenty-second' (Doane 1827). pp. 267–270: house-number-by-house-number list of 'South Side residents — Prairie Avenue' (e.g. 1936 S. W. Allerton; 2009 Mrs Sarah Meyer; 2013 W. H. Reid; 2100 J. B. Sherman; 2115 P. D. Armour; 2126 C. D. Hamill; 2130 Thomas Murdoch; 2140 Byron L. Smith) — useful to key the drawings to occupants c.1893. Page 229 carries a 'Route of South Side Drive' sketch map (Michigan Blvd → 16th St → Prairie Ave → south). Index lines quoted from IA OCR.

images.notes: Street-level view down Prairie Avenue across the 20th Street intersection, numbered '47' (probably a municipal/streetcar-era survey series). Paved roadway with crown, curbs with granite corners, cast-iron lamp-posts with globe lamps, parkway trees (leafless), large Romanesque/Queen Anne corner house at right marked by arrow (2001), stone mansions at left, street receding to a vanishing point. Useful for 1904 street surface and lighting (with care for 1904–1915 changes: electric lamps). Orientation and the identity of houses other than 2001 not verified.
